headline: Tonight's storm has shifted east, so New York City gets little or no rain, but a much bigger storm late Wednesday night through Friday will likely bring 1 to 2 inches of rain, gusts of 35 to 45 mph and widespread coastal flooding on Thanksgiving.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Low pressure now looks to pass just east of Long Island tonight, so New York City and areas north and west should see little to no rain, though a few spots just west of the main rain area could get some light rain. Far eastern Long Island and southeastern Connecticut get moderate to locally heavy rain, totaling 0.75 to 1 inch, mainly this evening into the early morning hours Monday. Because the storm is tracking farther east, winds will also be much weaker than earlier expected.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Any lingering rain leaves eastern areas Monday morning and skies clear, then a cold front passes in the afternoon with northwest gusts around 20 mph; Monday is another warm day in the 60s, though records around 70 are unlikely to fall (Islip has tied or broken its record high each of the last four days). Tuesday and Wednesday turn much cooler as an unusually strong area of high pressure builds to the north, with highs struggling to get out of the 40s and lows mostly below freezing, except in the New York City metro area Wednesday morning. Wednesday night, clouds lower and east-northeast winds increase, gusting 25 to 35 mph, highest around the city and along the coast, with a slight chance of rain late.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: A large storm system will likely bring rain, wind and widespread coastal flooding late Wednesday night into Friday, so escaping bad weather for Thanksgiving looks unlikely; the open question is how severe the impacts get. Winds are strongest during the day Thursday, with east-northeast winds of 20 to 30 mph and gusts of 35 to 45 mph, possibly 50 mph at the coast, and rain totals of 1 to 2 inches look reasonable since the storm moves along fairly quickly, though storms from the south this year carry plenty of moisture thanks to El Niño. Friday brings a lingering chance of rain mainly in the morning, with winds turning west and gusting around 30 to 35 mph.

coast: A minimal coastal flood threat at most exists for the south shore back bays of Nassau County and Queens with Monday morning's high tide; water levels will probably fall just short of minor flooding, and no statement is planned. Coastal flooding is growing more likely with the Thanksgiving storm, since a full moon on Tuesday the 24th and king tides this week mean many spots need less than a foot of extra water to flood; the current forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding Thursday, perhaps even localized major flooding, along with beach flooding, erosion and overwash. On the water, Gale Warnings for the outer ocean have been dropped with tonight's eastward storm track; a Small Craft Advisory covers eastern Long Island Sound (east of the Connecticut River) until 6 PM Monday and the near-shore ocean waters until 6 AM Tuesday because of large ocean waves and northwest winds. After a brief lull Tuesday afternoon and night, ocean gusts of about 29 to 35 mph (25 to 30 knots) return by Wednesday evening, reaching gale force Wednesday night and storm force Thursday, with gales on the Sound and bays late Wednesday night into Thursday; waves could peak at 15 to 20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20 to 25 feet out east), 7 to 10 feet on Long Island Sound, and around 10 feet on western Block Island Sound east of Orient Point.
watch_for: Thanksgiving storm: widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, possibly localized major, plus beach erosion and overwash, during king tides.
Thursday winds gusting 35 to 45 mph (up to 50 mph at the coast) and 1 to 2 inches of rain; the storm's exact track is still uncertain.
A sharp cutoff to tonight's rain: little to none in New York City versus up to an inch on far eastern Long Island.
confidence: Forecasters are fairly confident tonight's rain stays mostly over eastern Long Island and southeastern Connecticut, and confident a significant Thanksgiving storm is coming, but how severe its impacts will be, and whether the storm tracks farther west, remains uncertain.
